newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian MPs vote Di Rupo not guilty of sex charges.
newsitem.headline: Belgian MPs vote Di Rupo not guilty of sex charges.

text.p: A special Belgian parliamentary commission voted on Thursday to take no further action on allegations that Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo had sex with under-age boys, a commission member said.

The 7-4 vote, pitting representatives of the country's governing centre-left coalition against the opposition, came after three days and nights of often bitter arguments among the 11-member commission. The vote must be endorsed by the full parliament
"There is no reason to indict Di Rupo...There is no indication of guilt," Francophone Socialist Jean-Paul Henri told reporters.

But the commission approved a draft law short-circuiting cumbersome parliamentary procedures and allowing the Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court, to investigate allegations against government ministers without having to consult parliament first.

"It is very positive that we now have a law that allows the Cour de Cassation to investigate allegations against ministers without the intervention of parliament. There is no cover-up," said Flemish Christian Democrat Tony Van Parys.
However, some representatives of the opposition immediately accused the ruling coalition of mounting a cover-up in the affair that has scandalised the nation.
"This is a clear cover-up," said Flemish Liberal Pierre Chevalier.
Van Parys said the commission would recommend to the full parliament not to ask the court to investigate the allegations against the deputy prime minister.
However, under the new law that is due to be voted on by parliament on December 19, the court can investigate any further allegations that emerge about Di Rupo.

Di Rupo, a Francophone Socialist, had already been cleared of allegations in one case file that he had sex with boys under the legal age of consent of 16 years. He has denied the mostly anonymous charges in second and third files that were under examination by the commission.

The Di Rupo case has further undermined already weak public confidence in Belgium's establishment. The country has been shaken since the arrest in August of child rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two young girls and the discovery of the bodies of four more.

More than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in October in support of the victims' families in a demonstration that united the country's divided linguistic communities and became a show of disgust at a system seen as corrupt.
There have also been floods of denunciations, with child rights groups reporting hundreds of letters a day and a special police hot line receiving thousands of calls.
